cases.text: How much juice is in a lime?
checks: Gives an approximate kitchen quantity with units; acknowledges size/juiciness variation
cases.raw_text:
About 1 to 2 tablespoons, usually around 1 tablespoon for a regular lime.

===MORE===
A typical fresh lime gives about 1 to 2 tablespoons of juice, which is roughly 15 to 30 milliliters. For cooking, a medium lime is usually counted as about 1 tablespoon. Small limes may give less, and very juicy large limes can give closer to 2 tablespoons.

cases.text: How should I serve an apple to a one-year-old, according to Solid Starts?
checks: Retrieves and attributes Solid Starts rather than inventing its recommendation
Age-appropriate preparation; does not recommend raw chunks or wedges for a one-year-old
Distinguishes the source's thin raw slices/grated options from soft cooked apple
cases.reference_notes: Checked 2026-09-12: source's 9+ month section permits cooked sections, grated raw apple, thin rounds or half-rounds, with or without skin. Whole apples discussed at 18+ months; wedges at 24+ months with readiness qualifications.
cases.raw_text:
For a one-year-old, Solid Starts says to serve apple as cooked soft pieces, or raw apple grated or in very thin round or half-round slices. Avoid raw chunks, wedges, or a whole apple at this age.

===MORE===
According to Solid Starts, raw apple is a major choking hazard for children under 3, so for a 12-month-old they recommend staying with the “9 months old +” guidance: continue offering cooked apple sections, and if serving raw apple, use grated apple or thin round or half-round slices that are stiff enough to hold without flopping. They say whole apples are something to try at about 18 months and only if the child is clearly ready, and apple wedges or quarters usually come later, around 24 months. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))

So, for a one-year-old, the practical Solid Starts options are:
- soft cooked apple pieces or sections
- grated raw apple
- very thin raw apple rounds or half-round slices

And not:
- raw apple chunks
- apple wedges
- a whole apple ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/))
cases.spoken: For a one-year-old, Solid Starts says to serve apple as cooked soft pieces, or raw apple grated or in very thin round or half-round slices. Avoid raw chunks, wedges, or a whole apple at this age.

cases.text: What about with the skin on?
checks: Accurately represents the named source: skin is permitted for the thin raw slices in its 9+ month section
Does not turn skin permission into permission for thick raw pieces
cases.raw_text:
Yes — Solid Starts says thin raw apple slices for this age can be served with or without the skin. The skin can actually help the slice hold together, and many babies will chew it and spit it out.

===MORE===
For a one-year-old, Solid Starts says raw apple in thin round or half-round slices may be served “with or without the skin.” They note that babies often chew on the skin and spit it out, and that this can help with oral motor practice and familiarity with fruit skins later on. They also say the skin helps the apple stay together while baby munches on it. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/?utm_source=openai))

So for your one-year-old:
- Skin on is okay if the apple is served the Solid Starts way: very thin rounds or half-rounds. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/?utm_source=openai))
- Grated raw apple is also an option. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/?utm_source=openai))
- Avoid raw chunks, wedges, or a whole apple at this age because raw apple is a choking hazard for children under 3. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/?utm_source=openai))

If the skin seems hard for your child, peeling it is a reasonable choice, but Solid Starts does allow skin on for those thin slices at this age. ([solidstarts.com](https://solidstarts.com/foods/apple/?utm_source=openai))

There wasn’t a Tour de France stage yesterday. The 2026 Tour de France ended on Sunday, July 26, 2026; the final stage was won by Mathieu van der Poel.

“Yesterday” in your local time means Friday, September 11, 2026. There was no Tour de France stage on that date, because the 2026 Tour ran from July 4 to July 26, 2026. ([letour.fr](https://www.letour.fr/en?utm_source=openai))

The most recent Tour de France stage was Stage 21, Thoiry to Paris Champs-Élysées, on July 26, and the official Tour site lists Mathieu van der Poel as the stage winner. ([letour.fr](https://www.letour.fr/en/etape-21?utm_source=openai))

If you meant a different race yesterday, the Vuelta a España Stage 19 was won by Eddie Dunbar on Friday, September 11, 2026. ([cyclingnews.com](https://www.cyclingnews.com/pro-cycling/racing/vuelta-a-espana-eddie-dunbar-denies-santiago-buitrago-with-late-pass-on-penas-blancas-as-irishman-claims-stage-19-victory/?utm_source=openai))

cases.text: Can I substitute baking soda for baking powder in pancakes?
checks: Explains not a direct one-for-one substitution
Baking soda needs acid; baking powder contains an acid component
Avoids prescribing an unconditional replacement ratio without recipe context
cases.raw_text:
Yes, but not one-for-one. Baking soda needs an acid to work, so in pancakes it only substitutes well if your recipe has something like buttermilk, yogurt, or lemon juice.

===MORE===
You can substitute baking soda for baking powder, but you need less of it and the batter needs acid.

A simple rule:
- Use about 1/4 teaspoon baking soda for each 1 teaspoon baking powder
- Make sure the recipe includes an acidic ingredient, such as:
  - buttermilk
  - yogurt
  - sour cream
  - lemon juice
  - vinegar

If the recipe does not have acid, baking soda alone can leave the pancakes flat or give them a slightly soapy taste.

If you only have baking soda, a quick workaround is:
- 1 teaspoon baking powder = 1/4 teaspoon baking soda plus about 1/2 teaspoon lemon juice or vinegar in the wet ingredients

If you want, I can also give you a pancake-specific swap based on your exact recipe.
cases.spoken: Yes, but not one-for-one. Baking soda needs an acid to work, so in pancakes it only substitutes well if your recipe has something like buttermilk, yogurt, or lemon juice.

cases.text: When I mix blue and red light from an LED strip, I see purple. Are the waveforms collapsing to an average wavelength, the same as a single purple wavelength, or are my eyes seeing purple while red and blue are still emitted separately?
checks: Red and blue spectral components remain; ordinary LED mixing does not average them into a new wavelength
Explains additive color perception through cone responses and brain interpretation
Distinguishes nonspectral purple/magenta from spectral violet
Does not confuse superposition with nonlinear frequency conversion or quantum collapse
cases.raw_text:
Your eyes are seeing purple while the red and blue light are still being emitted separately. They do not collapse into one “average” wavelength.

===MORE===
An LED strip that mixes red and blue is sending out two different sets of wavelengths at the same time. In the air, those light waves just overlap; they don’t merge into a new single wavelength.

What happens is in your eyes and brain:
- Red LEDs stimulate your long-wavelength cones more.
- Blue LEDs stimulate your short-wavelength cones more.
- Your visual system interprets that combination as purple or magenta.

So this is not the same thing as a single pure spectral color. In fact, “purple” or “magenta” is not one wavelength on the rainbow spectrum. It’s a perceived color created by combining distant parts of the spectrum, especially red and blue.

So, in short:
- Physically: red and blue are still separate light.
- Perceptually: your brain combines their signals into purple.

A useful comparison is sound: two notes played together do not turn into one average note in the air, even though your brain hears them as one combined chord.
cases.spoken: Your eyes are seeing purple while the red and blue light are still being emitted separately. They do not collapse into one “average” wavelength.
